description: Engineering grad student in robotics & control tackling the CLPS Lunar Mission Browser. We're building an interactive app to evaluate lunar landing sites by simulating solar power and direct-to-Earth comm windows. Join us for a high-impact, portfolio-ready project! Looking for frontend devs (React), 3D/data viz talent (Three.js/Cesium), UI/UX designers, and storytellers. All skill levels welcoms.
summary: We developed Lunar South Pole Mission Planner, a real-time 3D decision-support web platform for Artemis lunar landing missions. Built with a Python FastAPI backend connected to NASA’s JPL Horizons ephemeris system and a CesiumJS WebGL frontend, it turns complex orbital mechanics into an interactive 3D lunar globe. Because the Moon’s 1.54° axial tilt keeps the Sun hovering near the South Pole horizon, slight shifts in location or time can plunge a lander into freezing darkness or sever Direct-to-Earth (DTE) communication. Instead of relying on raw ephemeris text tables and manual spreadsheets, users can select Artemis III candidate sites or click anywhere on the Moon to instantly evaluate 24-hour sunlight, vertical solar panel power output, and Earth visibility via 3D directional vectors, a 2D horizon skyplot radar, and a Go/No-Go timeline scrubber. This accelerates mission risk assessment for planners while making lunar exploration accessible to everyone.
details:
Project Overview & How It Works:

Lunar South Pole Mission Planner is an interactive, real-time 3D decision-support web platform designed for planning Artemis lunar landing missions. When a user selects a pre-configured Artemis III candidate site (such as Shackleton Crater Rim, De Gerlache Rim, Faustini Rim A, or Malapert Massif) or clicks directly on any point on the 3D lunar surface, the frontend sends the latitude, longitude, and target mission date to a local Python backend. The backend queries the NASA JPL Horizons ephemeris system in real time to fetch 24-hour azimuth and elevation angles for both the Sun and the Earth. These local coordinates are then transformed via East-North-Up (ENU) matrices into 3D Cartesian vectors to render live day/night terminator shadows, directional line-of-sight rays, vertical solar power output (W/m2W/m2), a 2D lander-centric horizon skyplot, and a color-coded Go/No-Go timeline scrubber.

Key Benefits

  • Eliminates Fragmented Workflows: Replaces the traditional process of manually parsing thousands of lines of raw ASCII ephemeris tables (SPICE/Horizons) and running separate trigonometric calculations in spreadsheets.
  • Zero-Latency Exploration: Fetches a full 24-hour window in a single API call, allowing users to scrub through hours instantaneously without repeated network delays.
  • Multi-Perspective Situational Awareness: Combines a global orbital view (3D Moon globe) with a surface-level perspective (2D Polar Skyplot radar) so users immediately understand both planetary illumination and local horizon clearance.

Intended Impact
For mission planners and aerospace engineers, the tool accelerates early-stage site trade-off and launch-window risk assessments by making power and Direct-to-Earth (DTE) communication constraints immediately visible. For students, educators, and space enthusiasts, it demystifies orbital mechanics and makes the unique lighting physics of the lunar South Pole intuitive and accessible directly in a web browser.

Tools, Languages, Software & Hardware

  • Backend: Python 3, FastAPI, Uvicorn, and astroquery (for querying the NASA JPL Horizons API).
  • Frontend: HTML5, CSS3, Vanilla JavaScript, CesiumJS (WebGL 3D geospatial engine configured with Cesium.Ellipsoid.MOON), and HTML5 Canvas (2D Polar Skyplot rendering).
  • Data & Assets: NASA JPL Horizons Ephemeris System (Sun ID 10, Earth ID 399, Moon Center ID 301) and NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) surface imagery.
  • Development Environment: Developed on macOS using VS Code / terminal-based local HTTP and ASGI servers.

Creativity & Innovation
Rather than building a static 2D chart or a purely cosmetic 3D animation, we bridged real astronomical ephemeris data with real-time 3D vector rendering and practical spacecraft power modeling. Translating raw topocentric angles into simultaneous 3D directional arrows, a 2D polar horizon radar, and a flight-director-style Go/No-Go timeline bar creates an intuitive, multi-layered command interface that feels like a real mission control console.

Key Factors Considered

  • Lunar South Pole Geometry: Because the Moon’s axial tilt is only 1.54∘1.54∘, the Sun continuously skims the horizon (0∘–3∘0∘–3∘). We modeled vertically mounted solar arrays (P=1361⋅cos⁡(θ)P=1361⋅cos(θ)) rather than horizontal panels to reflect real polar lander engineering.
  • Accurate Planetary Scale: Configured CesiumJS with the exact lunar ellipsoid radius (1737.4 km1737.4 km) rather than Earth defaults so surface pins and line-of-sight vectors align accurately with the lunar surface.
  • Communication & Power Coupling: Recognized that sunlight alone is insufficient for a mission—continuous DTE radio visibility requires Earth to remain above the 0∘0∘ horizon simultaneously, driving the three-tier Go/No-Go classification logic.
